sourceSentences.text: The next morning I arose and continued on my way.
Nighteyes had left me two days ago.
Only two days.
Yet it seemed very long to me that I had been alone.
And how, I wondered, did Nighteyes measure our separation?
Not by days and nights.
He had gone to find out a thing, and when he had found it out, then his time to be away from me would be over and he would come back to me.
But what, really, had he gone to find out?
What it was like to be a wolf among wolves, a member of a pack?
If they accepted him, what then?
Would he run with them for a day, a week, a season?
How long would it take for me to fade from his mind into one of his endless yesterdays?
Why should he want to return to me, if this pack would accept him?
After a time, I allowed myself to realize I was as heartsore and hurt as if a human friend had snubbed me for the company of others.
I wanted to howl, to quest out to Nighteyes with my loneliness for him.
By an effort of will, I did not.
He was not a pet dog, to be whistled to heel.
He was a friend and we had travelled together for a time.
What right did I have to ask him to give up a chance at a mate, at a true pack of his own, simply that he might be at my side?
None at all, I told myself.
None at all.
At noon I struck a trail that followed the bank.
By late afternoon I had passed several small farmsteads.
Melons and grain predominated.
A network of ditches carried river-water inland to the crops.
The sod houses were set well back from the river’s edge, probably to avoid flooding.
I had been barked at by dogs, and honked at by flocks of fat white geese, but had seen no folk close enough to hail.
The trail had widened to a road, with cart-tracks.
The sun was beating on my back and head from a clear blue sky.
High above me, I heard the shrill ki of a hawk.
I glanced up at him, wings open and still as he rode the sky.
He gave cry again, folded his wings and plummeted toward me.
Doubtless, he dived on some small rodent in one of the fields.
I watched him come at me, and only at the last moment realized I was truly his target.
I flung up an arm to shield my face just as he opened his wings.
I felt the wind of his braking.
For a bird his size, he landed quite lightly on my upflung arm.
His talons clenched painfully in my flesh.
My first thought was that he was a trained bird gone feral, who had seen me and somehow decided to return to man.
A scrap of leather dangling from one of his legs might be the remainder of jesses.
He sat blinking on my arm, a magnificent bird in every way.
I held him out from me to have a better look at him.
The leather on his leg secured a tiny scroll of parchment.
‘Can I have a look at that?’
I asked him aloud.
He turned his head to my voice and one gleaming eye stared at me.
It was Sleet.
Old Blood.
I could make no more of his thoughts than that, but it was enough.
I had never been much good with the birds at Buckkeep.
Burrich had finally bid me leave them alone, for my presence always agitated them.
Nevertheless, I quested gently toward his flame-bright mind.
He seemed quiet.
I managed to tug the tiny scroll loose.
The hawk shifted on my arm, digging his talons into fresh flesh.
Then, without warning, he lifted his wings and launched away from me into the air.
He spiralled up, beating heavily to gain altitude, cried once more his high ki, ki, and went sliding off down the sky.
I was left with blood trickling down my arm where his talons had scored my flesh, and one ringing ear from the beating of his wings as he launched.
I glanced at the punctures in my arm.
Then curiosity made me turn to the tiny scroll.
Pigeons carried messages, not hawks.
The handwriting was in an old style, tiny, thin and spidery.
The brightness of the sun made it even harder to read.
I sat down at the edge of the road and shaded it with my hand to study it.
The first words almost stilled my heart.
‘Old Blood greets Old Blood.’
The rest was harder to puzzle out.
The scroll was tattered, the spellings quaint, the words as few as would suffice.
The warning was from Holly, though I suspected Rolf had penned it.
King Regal actively hunted down Old Blood now.
To those he captured, he offered coins if they would help find a wolf – man pair.
They suspected Nighteyes and I were the ones he wanted.
Regal threatened death to those who refused.
There was a little more, something about giving my scent to others of Old Blood and asking that they aid me as they could.
The rest of the scroll was too tattered to read.
I tucked the scroll into my belt.
The bright day seemed edged with darkness now.
So Will had told Regal I yet lived.
And Regal feared me enough to set these wheels in motion.
Perhaps it was as well that Nighteyes and I had parted company for a time.
As twilight fell, I ascended a small rise on the riverbank.
Ahead of me, tucked into a bend of the river, were a few lights.
Probably another trading post or a ferry dock to allow farmers and herders easy passage across the river.
I watched the lights as I walked toward them.
Ahead there would be hot food, and people, and shelter for the night.
I could stop and have a word with the folk there if I wished.
I still had a few coins to call my own.
No wolf at my heels to excite questions, no Nighteyes lurking outside hoping no dogs would pick up his scent.
No one to worry about except myself.
Well, maybe I would.
Maybe I’d stop and have a glass and a bit of talk.
Maybe I’d learn how much farther it was to Tradeford, and hear some gossip of what went on there.
It was time I began formulating a real plan as to how I would deal with Regal.
It was time I began depending only on myself.

Почерк был старинный — мелкий, тонкий и паучий. Яркость солнца ещё больше затрудняла чтение. Я сел на краю дороги и заслонил свиток рукой, чтобы изучить его. Первые слова едва не остановили моё сердце. «Древняя Кровь приветствует Древнюю Кровь».

Остальное было труднее разобрать. Свиток был истрёпан, написание — старомодным, а слов ровно столько, сколько требовалось. Предупреждение было от Холли, хотя я подозревал, что записал его Рольф. Король Регал теперь деятельно охотился на Древнюю Кровь. Тем, кого он ловил, он предлагал монеты за помощь в поисках пары волк — человек. Они подозревали, что Регал ищет нас с Ночным Волком. Регал угрожал смертью тем, кто отказывался. Далее было ещё немного — что-то о том, что мой запах передадут другим из Древней Крови и попросят их помогать мне, чем смогут. Остальная часть свитка была слишком истрёпана, чтобы её прочесть. Я сунул свиток за пояс. Яркий день теперь словно обвели тьмой. Значит, Уилл сказал Регалу, что я всё ещё жив. И Регал достаточно боялся меня, чтобы запустить эти шестерёнки. Возможно, даже хорошо, что мы с Ночным Волком на время расстались.

Когда опустились сумерки, я поднялся на небольшой холм на берегу реки. Впереди, приютившись в речной излучине, горело несколько огоньков. Вероятно, ещё один торговый пост или паромная пристань, чтобы фермерам и пастухам было легче переправляться через реку. Я смотрел на огни, идя к ним. Впереди были горячая еда, люди и ночлег. Я мог остановиться и поговорить с тамошними людьми, если захочу. У меня всё ещё оставалось несколько собственных монет. Никакого волка у пят, который возбуждал бы вопросы, никакого Ночного Волка, таящегося снаружи в надежде, что ни одна собака не возьмёт его след. Некому было тревожиться, кроме самого себя. Что ж, может быть, я и остановлюсь. Может быть, выпью стаканчик и поболтаю. Может быть, узнаю, далеко ли ещё до Тредфорда, и услышу сплетни о том, что там происходит. Пора было начать составлять настоящий план, как мне справиться с Регалом.
Пора было начать полагаться только на самого себя.

paragraphPairs.sourceText: The next morning I arose and continued on my way. Nighteyes had left me two days ago. Only two days. Yet it seemed very long to me that I had been alone. And how, I wondered, did Nighteyes measure our separation? Not by days and nights. He had gone to find out a thing, and when he had found it out, then his time to be away from me would be over and he would come back to me. But what, really, had he gone to find out? What it was like to be a wolf among wolves, a member of a pack? If they accepted him, what then? Would he run with them for a day, a week, a season? How long would it take for me to fade from his mind into one of his endless yesterdays?
paragraphPairs.translatedText: На следующее утро я встал и продолжил путь. Ночной Волк покинул меня два дня назад. Всего два дня. Но мне казалось, что я один уже очень давно. И как, подумал я, Ночной Волк измеряет нашу разлуку? Не днями и ночами. Он ушёл выяснить что-то, и когда выяснит, тогда закончится время, которое ему надо провести вдали от меня, и он вернётся. Но что, в сущности, он ушёл выяснять? Каково это — быть волком среди волков, членом стаи? Если они примут его, что тогда? Будет ли он бегать с ними день, неделю, сезон? Сколько времени понадобится, чтобы я стёрся из его памяти, став одним из его бесконечных вчера?

paragraphPairs.sourceText: At noon I struck a trail that followed the bank. By late afternoon I had passed several small farmsteads. Melons and grain predominated. A network of ditches carried river-water inland to the crops. The sod houses were set well back from the river’s edge, probably to avoid flooding. I had been barked at by dogs, and honked at by flocks of fat white geese, but had seen no folk close enough to hail. The trail had widened to a road, with cart-tracks.
paragraphPairs.translatedText: В полдень я вышел на тропу, шедшую вдоль берега. К позднему полудню я миновал несколько маленьких ферм. Повсюду преобладали дыни и зерновые. Сеть канав несла речную воду вглубь полей, к посевам. Дерновые дома стояли далеко от края реки, вероятно, чтобы избежать наводнений. На меня лаяли собаки, на меня гоготали стаи жирных белых гусей, но людей достаточно близко, чтобы окликнуть, я не видел. Тропа расширилась в дорогу с колеями от телег.

paragraphPairs.sourceText: The sun was beating on my back and head from a clear blue sky. High above me, I heard the shrill ki of a hawk. I glanced up at him, wings open and still as he rode the sky. He gave cry again, folded his wings and plummeted toward me. Doubtless, he dived on some small rodent in one of the fields. I watched him come at me, and only at the last moment realized I was truly his target. I flung up an arm to shield my face just as he opened his wings. I felt the wind of his braking. For a bird his size, he landed quite lightly on my upflung arm. His talons clenched painfully in my flesh.
paragraphPairs.translatedText: С ясного голубого неба солнце било мне в спину и голову. Высоко надо мной я услышал пронзительное ки ястреба. Я взглянул на него: распахнув крылья, неподвижный, он плыл по небу. Он снова крикнул, сложил крылья и камнем ринулся ко мне. Несомненно, он нырнул за каким-то мелким грызуном в одном из полей. Я смотрел, как он летит на меня, и лишь в последний миг понял, что его настоящая цель — я. Я вскинул руку, чтобы заслонить лицо, как раз когда он расправил крылья. Я почувствовал ветер от его торможения. Для птицы таких размеров он сел на мою поднятую руку совсем легко. Его когти болезненно впились в мою плоть.

paragraphPairs.sourceText: My first thought was that he was a trained bird gone feral, who had seen me and somehow decided to return to man. A scrap of leather dangling from one of his legs might be the remainder of jesses. He sat blinking on my arm, a magnificent bird in every way. I held him out from me to have a better look at him. The leather on his leg secured a tiny scroll of parchment. ‘Can I have a look at that?’ I asked him aloud. He turned his head to my voice and one gleaming eye stared at me. It was Sleet.
paragraphPairs.translatedText: Сначала я подумал, что это обученная птица, одичавшая и, увидев меня, почему-то решившая вернуться к человеку. Кусочек кожи, свисавший с одной его лапы, мог быть остатком путцев. Он сидел, моргая, на моей руке — великолепная птица во всех отношениях. Я вытянул руку, чтобы лучше его рассмотреть. Кожа на его лапе удерживала крошечный свиток пергамента. «Можно мне взглянуть на это?» — спросил я его вслух. Он повернул голову на мой голос, и один сияющий глаз уставился на меня. Это был Слит.

paragraphPairs.sourceText: I had never been much good with the birds at Buckkeep. Burrich had finally bid me leave them alone, for my presence always agitated them. Nevertheless, I quested gently toward his flame-bright mind. He seemed quiet. I managed to tug the tiny scroll loose. The hawk shifted on my arm, digging his talons into fresh flesh. Then, without warning, he lifted his wings and launched away from me into the air. He spiralled up, beating heavily to gain altitude, cried once more his high ki, ki, and went sliding off down the sky. I was left with blood trickling down my arm where his talons had scored my flesh, and one ringing ear from the beating of his wings as he launched. I glanced at the punctures in my arm. Then curiosity made me turn to the tiny scroll. Pigeons carried messages, not hawks.
paragraphPairs.translatedText: Я никогда не особенно ладил с птицами в Баккипе. Наконец Баррич велел мне оставить их в покое, потому что моё присутствие всегда их тревожило. Тем не менее я мягко потянулся к его яркому, как пламя, разуму. Он казался спокойным. Мне удалось высвободить крошечный свиток. Ястреб переместился на моей руке, впиваясь когтями в свежий участок плоти. Затем без предупреждения он расправил крылья и взмыл с моей руки в воздух. Он по спирали поднялся вверх, тяжело работая крыльями, чтобы набрать высоту, ещё раз издал своё высокое ки, ки и скользнул прочь по небу. Я остался с кровью, струившейся по руке там, где когти распороли плоть, и с одним звенящим ухом от взмахов его крыльев при взлёте. Я взглянул на проколы на руке. Потом любопытство заставило меня повернуться к крошечному свитку. Послания носили голуби, не ястребы.

paragraphPairs.sourceText: As twilight fell, I ascended a small rise on the riverbank. Ahead of me, tucked into a bend of the river, were a few lights. Probably another trading post or a ferry dock to allow farmers and herders easy passage across the river. I watched the lights as I walked toward them. Ahead there would be hot food, and people, and shelter for the night. I could stop and have a word with the folk there if I wished. I still had a few coins to call my own. No wolf at my heels to excite questions, no Nighteyes lurking outside hoping no dogs would pick up his scent. No one to worry about except myself. Well, maybe I would. Maybe I’d stop and have a glass and a bit of talk. Maybe I’d learn how much farther it was to Tradeford, and hear some gossip of what went on there. It was time I began formulating a real plan as to how I would deal with Regal.
paragraphPairs.translatedText: Когда опустились сумерки, я поднялся на небольшой холм на берегу реки. Впереди, приютившись в речной излучине, горело несколько огоньков. Вероятно, ещё один торговый пост или паромная пристань, чтобы фермерам и пастухам было легче переправляться через реку. Я смотрел на огни, идя к ним. Впереди были горячая еда, люди и ночлег.
